title: How do you know where you are on the open sea?
new_ideas: a watch face that morphs into a globe (time becomes place) — the film's thesis as one transformation
two ships on one chart (believed vs real) as the cold-open mechanism
the opening's lanterns going out are relit along a safe course at the end (bookend)

lines.text: On a stormy night in October 1707, a fleet of British warships was sailing home, believing it was safely out in open *water*.

plan.see: Night storm at sea; a line of tall warships with lanterns lit, heeling in the wind; rain slants across.
plan.beats: +0.0 rise: the sea comes up from the bottom (1.4 s) | +1.6 the ships ink on in a line, swaying | +3.0 rain | +4.0 pan along the fleet

lines.text: Then, in the dark, the flagship struck the rocks of the Isles of Scilly, off the south-west tip of *England*.

plan.see: Black rocks rise out of the surf in front of the flagship's bow; a lantern swings wildly.
plan.beats: +0.0 drop: the rocks erupt from the sea (0.6 s, snap) | +0.8 the bow hits; tremble (1 s) · sfx timber crack −16 | +2.0 lanterns swing

lines.text: Four ships were lost. Somewhere between fourteen hundred and two thousand sailors *drowned*.

plan.see: Pull back: four lanterns on the dark water go out, one by one.
plan.beats: +0.0 pull back slowly (4 s) | +0.8 the lanterns go out one by one (0.8 s apart)

lines.text: Their admiral, Sir Cloudesley Shovell, was among the *dead*.

plan.see: A small framed portrait of the admiral lies face up on wet sand.
plan.beats: +0.0 slide: the portrait ★P-06 onto the sand | +1.4 a wave washes over its edge

lines.text: The fleet's officers had simply been wrong about where they *were*.

plan.see: A real chart of the Scilly approaches ★M-01 unrolls; a pencilled ship sits safe in open sea — and an inked ship lies on the rocks.
plan.beats: +0.0 unroll: ★M-01 (1.6 s) | +2.0 the 'believed' ship is pencilled in open sea | +3.2 the real wreck inks on the rocks | +4.2 a dashed line between them

lines.text: Some historians think their real mistake was in latitude, not longitude. Either way, out at sea, they had no reliable way to *check*.

plan.see: On the chart, a pencil circles the believed position with a question mark.
plan.beats: +0.0 quill circles the pencilled ship | +1.4 a '?' in the margin

lines.text: At sea, with no land in sight, how do you know where you *are*?

plan.see: A small boat on a perfectly round, empty horizon; the sea in every direction looks the same.
plan.beats: +0.0 wipe: the empty horizon (1.4 s) | +1.6 orbit: the camera circles the boat (5 s); nothing changes

lines.text: Every position on Earth has two numbers: how far north or south — latitude — and how far east or west — *longitude*.

plan.see: A globe; parallels ink on in gold, then meridians in red; their crossing marks one point.
plan.beats: +0.0 grow: parallels (1.6 s) | +2.2 meridians (1.6 s) | +4.2 a pin at a crossing

lines.text: Latitude was easy. The height of the Sun at noon, or of the Pole Star at night, tells you how far north you *are*.

plan.see: A navigator on deck holds a quadrant up to the Pole Star; the angle is drawn between horizon and star.
plan.beats: +0.0 slide: the navigator (Person, 1700s seaman) | +1.4 tilt up to the Pole Star | +2.6 an angle arc with a label

lines.text: But longitude had no star to look at. East and west, the sky looks the *same*.

plan.see: Pan east to west across the same sky: no fixed mark.
plan.beats: +0.0 pan (4 s) | +0.4 blinds: the same sky strip repeats

lines.text: So sailors guessed. They estimated speed and direction, and drew their path on a chart — and the errors grew every *day*.

plan.see: A pencilled track on a chart; a fan of uncertainty widens around it day by day.
plan.beats: +0.0 quill draws the track (3 s) | +1.0 a widening grey fan follows it

lines.text: Captains often sailed to the right latitude first, then followed it east or west until land appeared — slow, crowded, and *dangerous*.

plan.see: A gold band of latitude across the ocean chart, crowded with small ships following it in a line.
plan.beats: +0.0 grow: the band (1.4 s) | +1.6 ships ride along it in single file (trail ×5)

lines.text: Finding longitude became one of the great unsolved problems of the age — and the answer would come down to a single *question*.

plan.see: A blank card on the chart; a question mark is stamped on it.
plan.beats: +0.0 stamp '?' (snap) | +1.0 push

lines.text: Our first clue is a *clock*.

plan.see: Clue tag 1/4; title 'Clue I · The Missing Clock'.
plan.beats: +0.0 clue tag 1 | +0.2 title

lines.text: The Earth turns once a day: three hundred and sixty degrees in twenty-four *hours*.

plan.see: The globe turns; around it, a clock dial of twenty-four hours inks on.
plan.beats: +0.0 orbit: the globe turns (5 s) | +1.2 grow: a 24-hour dial rings it

lines.text: So every hour of difference in time means fifteen degrees of longitude, east or *west*.

plan.see: One hour on the dial lights up, and a slice of the globe between two meridians fills with gold.
plan.beats: +0.0 one hour segment lights | +1.0 wipe: a 15° slice fills | +2.4 label '1 hour = 15°'

lines.text: At sea, you can find your local noon from the Sun. If you also knew the time back home at that same moment, the difference would give you your *longitude*.

plan.see: Split: a ship at sea, the Sun at its highest; and a clock in London showing three in the afternoon.
plan.beats: +0.0 slide in both halves | +2.0 the Sun reaches noon over the ship | +3.6 the London clock reads 3 o'clock | +5.0 note '3 hours → 45° west'

lines.text: The problem was the second clock. No clock in the world could keep good time on a rolling *ship*.

plan.see: A tall pendulum clock stands on a heaving deck; its pendulum swings wildly, stops, swings again.
plan.beats: +0.0 drop: the clock on deck | +1.0 the deck rolls; the pendulum jerks (tremble) | +3.0 it stops

lines.text: And a clock that drifted by just a few seconds a day would, over a long voyage, put a ship many miles off *course*.

plan.see: A clock face whose minute hand doubles and fans out as days pass; on the chart, the ship's mark drifts with it.
plan.beats: +0.0 blinds: days pass (×6) | +1.6 the hand fans out | +3.0 the ship mark slides off course

lines.text: Pendulums swung wildly with the waves. Heat and cold made metal stretch and shrink. Damp air and salt slowed the *works*.

plan.see: Three small vignettes: a wave, a thermometer swinging from tropical heat to ice, salt crusting on brass gears.
plan.beats: +0.0 assemble: three vignettes (0.8 s each) | +3.0 each one clouds a small clock face

lines.text: Many of the best scientists in Europe agreed: a sea clock that good was *impossible*.

plan.see: A red stamp 'IMPOSSIBLE' lands across the clock vignettes.
plan.beats: +0.0 stamp 'Impossible' (snap)

lines.text: Clue two: a *prize*.

plan.see: Clue tag 2/4; title 'Clue II · A Fortune for an Answer'.
plan.beats: +0.0 clue tag 2 | +0.2 title

lines.text: In 1714, the British Parliament passed the Longitude Act. It offered up to twenty thousand pounds for a practical way to find longitude at *sea*.

plan.see: The real printed Act ★D-01 unrolls; the sum is circled; a tall stack of gold coins builds beside it.
plan.beats: +0.0 unroll: ★D-01 (1.6 s) | +2.0 red circle round '£20,000' | +3.0 coins stack up (drop, stagger) · sfx coins −22

lines.text: The Act set up a Board of Longitude to judge every idea. Who would *win*?

plan.see: A long table appears with empty chairs and an inkwell at every place.
plan.beats: +0.0 assemble: chairs slide in around a table (stagger) | +2.0 inkwells drop

lines.text: In fact, no one would ever be paid the full prize — not even the man who *earned* it.

plan.see: A small tear runs through the corner of the printed Act.
plan.beats: +0.0 a tear creeps across the Act's corner (1.2 s)

lines.text: A fortune: many lifetimes of a sailor's *wages*.

plan.see: The coin stack towers over a tiny sailor beside it.
plan.beats: +0.0 scale-out: a small sailor appears at the stack's foot

lines.text: But the method had to fix a ship's position to within half a degree, and prove it on a voyage across the *ocean*.

plan.see: On a sea chart, a small target circle half a degree wide around a ship.
plan.beats: +0.0 iris: the chart and a small target ring (1.2 s) | +1.6 label 'half a degree'

lines.text: Historians now doubt that the Scilly disaster led directly to that prize. But everyone knew what being lost at sea could *cost*.

plan.see: The wreck scene returns faintly behind the chart; the chart tears away from it.
plan.beats: +0.0 the wreck scene fades in under the chart (sepia) | +2.4 tear-away

lines.text: Ideas poured in. One proposed a line of ships anchored across the ocean, firing signals at fixed times for every sailor to *hear*.

plan.see: A comic but true proposal drawn straight: anchored ships in a row across the Atlantic, each firing a rocket at the same moment.
plan.beats: +0.0 drop: anchored ships in a line (stagger 0.2 s) | +2.0 rockets burst in sequence (ripple) | +3.4 whip back to the board

lines.text: Astronomers had their own answer. They would use the Moon as a clock in the *sky*.

plan.see: The Moon rises over the sea among bright stars; it creeps visibly against them.
plan.beats: +0.0 rise: the Moon (1.6 s) | +1.8 it creeps across the stars (trail, 4 s)

lines.text: The Moon moves steadily against the stars. Measure the angle between the Moon and a bright star, look it up in tables, and you get the time back *home*.

plan.see: A sextant raised to the sky; a gold angle opens between the Moon and a star; the angle points to a row in a printed table.
plan.beats: +0.0 a sextant inks on | +1.4 grow: the angle between Moon and star | +3.4 the angle drops onto a table row

lines.text: But the sums were long and hard, and the tables had to be *right*.

plan.see: A navigator in a candlelit cabin, sheets of figures spread around him.
plan.beats: +0.0 slide: the cabin | +1.4 papers multiply around him

lines.text: On a pitching deck, a tiny slip in measuring that angle could throw the answer off by many *miles*.

plan.see: The sextant on a pitching deck; the gold angle wobbles; the chart mark jumps.
plan.beats: +0.0 slide: the deck tilts | +1.0 the angle trembles | +2.4 the mark jumps on the chart

lines.text: In 1767, the Astronomer Royal, Nevil Maskelyne, published a Nautical Almanac full of ready-made Moon tables. Hours of work shrank to about *one*.

plan.see: The real almanac page ★D-02 lands on the papers; the pile of sums shrinks into one sheet; Maskelyne's portrait pinned.
plan.beats: +0.0 ★D-02 drops in | +1.4 the pile collapses into one sheet (collapse) | +3.0 ★P-07 small plate

lines.text: Clue three: a *carpenter*.

plan.see: Clue tag 3/4; title 'Clue III · The Carpenter's Clocks'.
plan.beats: +0.0 clue tag 3 | +0.2 title

lines.text: Far from London, in the north of England, a carpenter named John Harrison had taught himself to build *clocks*.

plan.see: A village workshop of wood shavings and tools; a young man planes a small wooden gear; his later portrait pinned on the wall.
plan.beats: +0.0 unroll: the workshop (1.6 s) | +1.8 Harrison (Person, 1720s working clothes) planing a gear | +3.4 ★P-04 cabinet card

lines.text: He was born in Yorkshire in 1693, a carpenter's son, and learned the trade from his *father*.

plan.see: A Yorkshire cottage at dusk; a boy watches his father at a bench.
plan.beats: +0.0 wipe: the cottage | +1.4 light-change: dusk warms

lines.text: His first clocks were made almost entirely of wood — and yet they kept astonishingly good *time*.

plan.see: A wooden movement fills the frame: oak gears turning, the grain of the wood visible.
plan.beats: +0.0 grow: the wooden gears ink on (2 s) | +2.0 they turn (life: rot)

lines.text: He invented a pendulum built of two different metals, so that heat and cold cancelled each other *out*.

plan.see: A gridiron pendulum of brass and steel rods; as heat glows red, some rods lengthen up and others down; the bob stays put.
plan.beats: +0.0 grow: the gridiron (1.6 s) | +2.0 heat wash: rods stretch in opposite directions; the bob does not move

lines.text: He chose hard, oily tropical wood for parts that rubbed together, so they needed no oil that would thicken and *fail*.

plan.see: Close on gear teeth in dark, oily wood, turning without a drop of oil.
plan.beats: +0.0 iris: the teeth close up | +1.4 morph: the wood darkens to lignum vitae

lines.text: When he heard about the prize, he set out to build a clock that could survive the *sea*.

plan.see: A printed notice of the prize slides onto his bench; he looks up from it.
plan.beats: +0.0 slide: the notice | +1.4 Harrison pose → look up

lines.text: In London, the famous clockmaker George Graham saw his designs, lent him money, and told him to keep *going*.

plan.see: A London shop of fine clocks; an older clockmaker hands young Harrison a purse.
plan.beats: +0.0 slide: the shop (1.2 s) | +1.6 a purse passes between them

lines.text: His first sea clock, H1, took about five years. It was a big brass machine, with two swinging balance arms in place of a *pendulum*.

plan.see: H1 rises: a box of brass with two dumbbell balances rocking against each other; the real photo ★P-01 pinned beside.
plan.beats: +0.0 rise: H1 (2 s) | +2.2 the balances rock in opposition | +3.6 ★P-01

lines.text: In 1736, it went to Lisbon on a navy ship, and on the way home it did better than the ship's own navigator. But the Board was not *convinced*.

plan.see: A ship sails out and back across a chart; on the return, the clock's position sits true while the navigator's pencil mark is far off.
plan.beats: +0.0 drop: the ship on the chart | +1.0 ride along the track (3 s) | +3.4 two marks: the clock's (gold) and the navigator's (pencil)

lines.text: But Harrison was never satisfied. He spent the next twenty years building two more *clocks*.

plan.see: H1, H2 and H3 stand side by side; the seasons change through the workshop window behind them.
plan.beats: +0.0 assemble: H2 and H3 slide in beside H1 | +2.4 seasons cycle in the window (light-change)

lines.text: H3 alone took him almost twenty years. He kept finding new problems, and he would not stop until each one was *solved*.

plan.see: Close on H3's caged roller bearing, newly invented; the workshop's light cycles day after day.
plan.beats: +0.0 iris: H3 detail | +1.6 light-change: days pass in the window

lines.text: Then he changed direction completely, and made something small enough to hold in your *hand*.

plan.see: The three big machines step back; in front of them, on a hand, a large silver watch: H4.
plan.beats: +0.0 the big clocks fade back | +1.2 bloom: H4 on a hand | +2.6 push

lines.text: Clue four: a watch at *sea*.

plan.see: Clue tag 4/4; title 'Clue IV · The Watch at Sea'.
plan.beats: +0.0 clue tag 4 | +0.2 title

lines.text: H4 looked like an oversized pocket watch. Inside, it was a jewel of tiny, fast-beating *parts*.

plan.see: The watch's back opens; a loupe moves over the movement; real close-ups ★P-02 and footage ★V-02.
plan.beats: +0.0 flip: the case back opens (flipY) | +1.4 Loupe over ★P-02 | +3.0 ★V-02 in the loupe

lines.text: Its balance swung back and forth about five times every second — far too fast for the roll of a ship to *upset* it.

plan.see: A fast-oscillating balance wheel in the foreground; behind it, a slow rolling deck.
plan.beats: +0.0 bloom: the balance beats fast (loop) | +1.6 the deck rolls slowly behind

lines.text: In 1761, his son William took it aboard HMS Deptford, bound for *Jamaica*.

plan.see: A ship sails off across the Atlantic chart; a young man in the cabin holds a small wooden box.
plan.beats: +0.0 slide: HMS Deptford leaves Portsmouth | +1.6 ride with the ship across the chart (4 s) | +3.0 window: William with the box

lines.text: The voyage took weeks. Every day, the watch was wound and checked, sealed in its box and guarded like treasure. Would it hold through the heat and the *storms*?

plan.see: In the cabin: day and night alternate through the porthole; a key winds the watch; the box closes and is locked.
plan.beats: +0.0 blinds: day/night through the porthole ×4 | +2.0 the key winds | +3.4 the lock clicks

lines.text: When the ship reached Jamaica, its longitude was checked from land. The watch had lost only a few *seconds*.

plan.see: Port Royal harbour; the watch beside a land clock; their hands nearly match; a gold figure 'a few seconds'.
plan.beats: +0.0 the harbour inks on | +1.6 match: the watch and the land clock side by side | +3.2 figure 'a few seconds' in gold

lines.text: A second trial, to Barbados in 1764, came out just as *well*.

plan.see: A second route draws across the chart to Barbados; the gold mark lands true again.
plan.beats: +0.0 slide: the chart shifts | +0.8 ride along the second route (3 s) | +3.0 gold mark on Barbados

lines.text: After weeks at sea, the ship's position was right to within a couple of *miles*.

plan.see: On the chart, the watch's position lands almost exactly on Jamaica.
plan.beats: +0.0 quill marks the watch's position on Jamaica (1 s)

lines.text: The prize should have been his. It *wasn't*.

plan.see: The stack of gold coins from clue two shrinks away from his reach.
plan.beats: +0.0 the coin stack slides away (collapse)

lines.text: The Board of Longitude, full of astronomers who favoured the Moon, demanded more trials, more tests, and his *drawings*.

plan.see: A long table of gentlemen in wigs; papers pass down it; a real Board page ★D-03 pinned.
plan.beats: +0.0 unroll: the board room (1.6 s) | +2.0 papers pass hand to hand | +3.4 ★D-03

lines.text: Why would they trust a watch? They even took it away from him, and had it taken apart in front of a panel of *experts*.

plan.see: H4's parts are laid out in an exploded view across the board table.
plan.beats: +0.0 tear-in: the case opens and parts spread (stagger) | +2.4 tremble

lines.text: Years went by. Copies of the watch were made, and still the doubts only slowly *faded*.

plan.see: A second watch, a copy, appears beside H4; the board's papers fade.
plan.beats: +0.0 assemble: K1 slides in beside H4 | +2.0 the papers fade (sepia)

lines.text: Captain James Cook carried one of those copies on his second great voyage, and in his journal called it 'our trusty friend the *Watch*'.

plan.see: Cook's ship in icy southern seas; the copy watch in his cabin; a real journal page ★D-04 slides in with a line underlined.
plan.beats: +0.0 drop: the ship among ice | +1.6 Cook (Person, naval coat) beside the watch | +3.2 ★D-04 with underline

lines.text: In 1773, at the urging of King George the Third, Parliament awarded the old carpenter a large sum. The Board never paid him the *prize*.

plan.see: Harrison, now old, receives a sealed paper; the empty prize-stack outline stays empty.
plan.beats: +0.0 stamp: a wax seal on a paper | +1.6 old Harrison (Person, age .8) | +3.0 the dotted outline of the prize stays empty

lines.text: Look at what the answer turned out to be. To know where you were, you had to know what time it *was*.

plan.see: The watch face morphs into the globe with its meridians; the hour hand becomes a meridian line.
plan.beats: +0.0 morph: watch face → globe (2 s) | +2.2 the hour hand becomes a meridian

lines.text: And that is still true. Every time your phone shows your position, it is reading clocks in *space*.

plan.see: Pull back from the globe to a ring of satellites around it; tiny pulses of time flow down to a phone in a hand.
plan.beats: +0.0 scale-out (3 s) | +1.4 rise: satellites on their orbits | +3.0 pulses flow to a phone (trail) | +4.0 ★V-03 in an OldScreen

lines.text: Satellites carry atomic clocks and broadcast the exact time. Your phone compares the signals — and turns time into *place*.

plan.see: Signals from three satellites arrive at slightly different moments; their circles cross at one point on the map.
plan.beats: +0.0 three rings of signal grow from three satellites (ripple) | +2.4 they cross at one dot

lines.text: Those clocks are so precise that if they drifted by even a millionth of a second, your phone would put you in the wrong *street*.

plan.see: On a phone's map, a pin jumps from one street to the next.
plan.beats: +0.0 the pin jumps (snap) | +1.0 jumps back

lines.text: So — how do you know where you are on the open *sea*?

plan.see: The small boat on the round empty horizon from the opening.
plan.beats: +0.0 wipe back to the boat | +1.0 orbit

lines.text: You carry home with you, in a watch. You find noon where you are. The difference in time is your *longitude*.

plan.see: On the boat, the navigator opens the watch at noon; a meridian line is drawn from the boat to the pole.
plan.beats: +0.0 drop: the watch in his hand | +1.6 the Sun at noon | +3.0 a meridian is drawn through the boat

lines.text: Harrison's clocks still tick at the Royal Observatory in Greenwich — the place the world's longitudes are counted *from*.

plan.see: A gallery with the four timekeepers in cases; outside the window, the meridian line on the ground.
plan.beats: +0.0 unroll: the gallery (1.6 s) | +2.0 pan past H1→H4 | +3.6 ★P-08 the meridian line

lines.text: Every ship that reaches port, every plane that lands in fog, every ambulance that finds the right door still uses his idea. Carry the time, and you will know the *place*.

plan.see: Ride past a ship docking, a plane descending through cloud, an ambulance at a door; a tiny clock glows in each.
plan.beats: +0.0 assemble: three vignettes (0.8 s each) | +2.4 ride across them | +4.6 tiny clocks glow in each

lines.text: A carpenter, who never went to university, gave every ship on Earth a way *home*.

plan.see: The night sea of the opening; one by one, ship lanterns light along a safe course; the brand end card follows.
plan.beats: +0.0 iris to the night sea | +1.4 lanterns light up along a course (stagger) | +4.0 end card
